We might phrase our current state-of-the-art knowledge that "All swans are white" as, "It would be legitimate to declare black swans empirically impossible."

So we have two things here: cognition and consciousness.

The first term, cognition, is a functional term. We can build computers which perform cognitive functions, by processes reasoning, through symbol manipulation, and alteration of storage to memory.

The second term, consciousness, is a nonfunctional term. It is claimed we don't know how to build computers which are conscious, or that we don't know how to know if we have built conscious computers.

A functional process has some kind of straightforward relationship between its mechanism and its function. So, for example, if a nerve firing is supposed to detect heat damage to your skin so that you recoil your hand from the stove, the function is detecting damage and avoiding it. This avoidance behavior seems perfectly required in order to achieve the function of damage avoidance. It is hard to imagine a function which would protect against heat damage without recoil, but even if there were such a function, however it works would make sense. Since that mechanism and behavior is researchable experimentally and empirically and physically, we can readily see how such a mechanism would evolve, to favor organisms with better and better versions of that mechanism.

A nonfunctional process has no such straightforward relationship between its mechanism and its function. So, consider seeing a STOP sign, or a red light. This redness quale signals you to stop. There is the mechanism on the left-hand side: the quale, and the function on the right-hand side: stopping. But unlike the intimate connection between recoil and damage avoidance, there seems to be no connection between the redness quale and the stopping. Of course, there is a cognitive element involved here. Red is recognized as a signal, that signal is interpreted to mean stop, and so you stop. But crucially, that redness quale was arbitrary. The STOP signs could have been blue, or appeared blue to you, and the function would have come out the same. We're left wondering how physical evolution can result in experiencing certain qualia in response to certain stimulus, when there seems to be no good reason why that qualia should be associated with that stimulus rather than another. Let's consider pain and its quale. Clearly nociception has an evolutionary function, but what about pain? Maybe nociception is automatic, unconscious, and reactive, where as pain is slow, conscious, and deliberative. And that also might have evolutionary benefit as opposed to mere reaction. But the question reminds why the feeling of pain on the left-hand side ought to be associated with the function of damage avoidance. If pain is only to act like a signal to alert consciousness or cognition about damage, so that you may deliberate upon it rather than merely reacting to it, there is no reason why pain had to feel "that way" in order to achieve that effect. Couldn't "pain" have come along with redness quale, itchiness, a loud middle C note, or coldness? Couldn't, say, coldness and pain be reversed? Such that when you're outside in the winter, you feel pain, but when you hit your hand with a hammer, you feel cold? All that is achieved by the signal is some kind of response to the stimulus, but the signal itself seems arbitrary for causing that response. In my first example with the hand recoiling from the hot stove, perhaps that mechanism was arbitrary, and the hand could have been protected by maybe releasing liquid or something. Just something different. Then you would claim the mechanism and the effect are arbitrary, but that's not so. The mechanism is not arbitrarily connected with the effect, because however the "spray liquid" mechanism would work, it would be seen to make sense as an explanation for how that mechanism achieves avoidance of heat damage. With qualia, that is not the case. We can admit that pain or coldness, whichever we have in whichever situation, does lead to some kind of response to the environment, but it still appears completely arbitrary why that original signal ought to be associated with that effect.

The cognitive component is describable and investigatable in terms of physical processes. A determined neuroscientist could study the behavior in the brain and completely explain what caused the person to fail to recognize themself in the mirror.

But then there is the qualitative component of looking in the mirror. There are the colors associated with the skin and hair.

When we say that one theory reduces another theory, it means something like all of the benefits we had from the older theory are maintained by the newer theory, and perhaps the newer theory even offers us additional benefits some how. The newer theory completely explains the older theory, but the older theory does not completely explain the newer theory. There are different working definitions for what "reduction" means.

When we say qualia are irreducible, we mean that nothing in the newer theory of neuroscience can explain the results in our "older theory" of our conscious experience. Neuroscience uses words like neuron, neurotransmitter, and synapse. And there seems to be no arrangement of that physical neurological stuff which ought imply qualia.

Contrast this with a Lego building. By specifying exactly where every Lego piece is, the building is explained. Things like the height of the building and the mass of the building can be determined through analysis of its constituent components. It makes sense that the height of the building is reducible to the height of the individual Lego pieces summed. It makes sense that the mass of the building is reducible to the mass of the individual Lego pieces summed. The atomic theory of Lego pieces reduces the composite theory of Lego buildings.

With qualia, what we take to be the "atomic primitives" of neuroscience are things like neurons and synapses and neurotransmitters, but unlike summing the heights of the individual Lego pieces to determine the height of the tower, there seems to be no mathematical function we can consider about the configuration of those neurons which ought in any way explain to us why we see red or feel pain. Simply, redness is not made up out of neurons. Pain is not made up out of neurons. Redness and pain are not made up out of neural processes, or at least that would be the dualist claim.

When we speak of qualia as irreducible, we are usually talking about its reduction not only specifically to neuroscientific items like neurons, but more generally to "structure and function." The dualist claim is that nothing about the "structure" or the "function" of any physical thing can ever, even in principle, reduce qualitative phenomena like redness and pain.

While the height of the Legos is a physical measurement, and the height of the tower is a physical measurement, and they are plainly reducible... The physical information about the configuration and behavior of neurons does not add up to a quale. A quale seems to lack physical features such as dimension, mass, location, perhaps quantity and duration.

When you see redness, you can claim things about your brain: what the mass of your brain is, where you brain is located in spacetime, why your brain ought to obey gravity... but you can't make those equivalent claims to the correlated phenomenological redness. This redness does not have mass or dimension or location. You can point out where in spacetime your brain is, but you can't point out where in spacetime your redness is.

What I just said was more of an explanation of irreducibility in terms of structure, whereas what I said before about STOP signs and red lights was the explanation of irreducibility in terms of function. Since whatever function our qualia are correlated with performing seem arbitrary, and that qualia can be swapped with any other arbitrary signalling qualia, we can find no explanation for why that qualia is correlated with that physical effect or how this could come to evolve at all. Evolution only works on the physical, such as brains, and it is hard to see how evolution can select for the nonphysical, such as qualia.

These terms are controversial. Some will call qualia physical. Some will call qualia reducible. Some will deny that qualia exist. But generally, when this terminology is used, its used in the dualist sense: it is taken for granted as charity to the dualist that we humans are like them and agree with them or at least can somewhat agree with them, that there seems to be a real puzzle about the relationship between physical damage and phenomological pain, in a way that there seems to be no real puzzle about the relationship between physical damage and recoil.

So we have prima facie evidence that qualia and the physical are distinct. Dualists think this first-person experiential evidence counts as a datum on the table to be considered. Physicalist/Scientistic types who do not trust the reliability of introspection or first-person accounts do not accept this "seeming" of qualia to be a datum on the table.
